questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart; definition; bar chart; timeline visualization
questions.text: A project manager uses a Gantt chart to communicate schedule status to the team. What does a Gantt chart show?

answers.text: A horizontal bar chart that plots project activities against a timeline — each bar's length represents the activity's duration; bars are arranged vertically by activity name; the chart shows planned start/end dates, actual progress (percentage complete bars), and relationships between activities
A hierarchical breakdown of all project deliverables organized by level
A probability-impact grid that maps project risks by likelihood and severity
A pie chart showing the percentage of budget allocated to each project phase

explanations.a: GANTT CHART: the most widely used project schedule visualization tool. KEY CHARACTERISTICS: HORIZONTAL BAR CHART: each project activity appears as a horizontal bar; the bar's LEFT EDGE = planned start date; the bar's RIGHT EDGE = planned end date; bar LENGTH = planned duration; TIMELINE AXIS: the horizontal axis is a calendar (days, weeks, months); activities are listed vertically on the left axis; PROGRESS TRACKING: many Gantt tools show a 'progress bar' within each activity bar (e.g., 60% shaded = 60% complete); DEPENDENCIES: dependency lines connect related activities (showing which activities must precede others); MILESTONES: shown as diamond shapes (zero duration) at key completion points; BASELINES: many tools overlay the original planned dates (baseline) against current dates for variance comparison. WHAT GANTT SHOWS AT A GLANCE: which activities are active right now; which are complete; which are not yet started; which are behind schedule (actual end date exceeds planned end date); the overall project timeline. GANTT LIMITATIONS: complex dependency relationships can be hard to read; doesn't show statistical probability of durations (PERT does); not ideal for showing the critical path calculation (network diagram does).
explanations.b: A hierarchical deliverable breakdown is the WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) — a scope tool, not a schedule visualization tool.
explanations.c: A probability-impact grid is a RISK MANAGEMENT tool (risk matrix) — not a schedule visualization.
explanations.d: A pie chart showing budget allocation is a COST tracking visualization — not a schedule chart.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — milestone chart; key events; executive reporting
questions.text: A project manager creates a milestone chart for the steering committee. What does a milestone chart show and why is it appropriate for executive audiences?

answers.text: A milestone chart shows only significant project events (milestones) against a timeline — no task-level detail; milestones are key completion events such as phase completions, deliverable approvals, and major go/no-go decision points; executives need the high-level status without operational detail
Milestone charts show every task in the project with daily granularity — more detail for executives
Milestone charts show resource allocation by team member — who is doing what on which date
Milestone charts are identical to Gantt charts — same tool, different name

explanations.a: MILESTONE CHART characteristics and executive suitability: WHAT IT SHOWS: significant project events only — no task-level detail; each milestone is a single point on the timeline (a date, not a duration range); typically includes 8-15 milestones for a large project (vs. hundreds of tasks in a full schedule); MILESTONE EXAMPLES: Phase 1 Requirements Complete (planned: March 15 | actual: March 18 — 3 days late); Architecture Review Approved (planned: April 1 | status: On Track); UAT Start (planned: June 1 | risk: vendor delay may impact); Final Go-Live (planned: September 30); VISUAL FORMAT: points or diamonds on a timeline; often color-coded: GREEN = on track or complete; AMBER = at risk; RED = delayed; STATUS AT A GLANCE: executives can see in 5 seconds which milestones are complete, on track, or at risk; WHY APPROPRIATE FOR EXECUTIVES: respects executives' limited time; focuses on decisions and strategic-level status; doesn't require understanding of task dependencies or technical detail; easily updated (8-15 milestones vs. 200 tasks); CONTRAST WITH GANTT: a Gantt chart shows all activities with durations and task-level detail — appropriate for the project team; a milestone chart shows only key events — appropriate for governance.
explanations.b: Executives don't need daily task granularity — they need strategic-level status. A 200-task Gantt chart overwhelms executives with information they cannot use to make decisions.
explanations.c: Resource allocation by team member is shown in a resource histogram or resource calendar — not a milestone chart.
explanations.d: Milestone charts and Gantt charts are distinct tools: Gantt shows all activities with durations; milestone chart shows only key events as points in time.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — burndown chart; Agile tracking; sprint velocity
questions.text: An Agile team uses a burndown chart during sprint execution. What does a burndown chart show?

answers.text: A burndown chart shows the amount of REMAINING WORK (in story points or hours) plotted against time within a sprint or release — the line 'burns down' from the total work at the sprint start to zero at the sprint end; an ideal burndown line shows linear progress; the actual line shows real team progress
Burndown charts show the total cost spent on the project over time — financial burn rate
Burndown charts show team member availability by day — who is present and who is absent
Burndown charts show the number of defects remaining after each testing cycle

explanations.a: BURNDOWN CHART in Agile: PURPOSE: track sprint (or release) progress against the goal of completing all committed work by the end of the sprint/release. AXES: Y-AXIS: remaining work (in story points, hours, or tasks); starts at the total work committed to at sprint start (e.g., 40 story points); X-AXIS: time (sprint days 1-10 for a 2-week sprint); IDEAL BURNDOWN LINE: a straight diagonal line from total work (Day 1) to zero (last day); shows what linear daily progress would look like; ACTUAL BURNDOWN LINE: the team's real progress; ideally tracks close to the ideal line; INTERPRETATION: actual line ABOVE ideal → team is behind (more work remaining than ideal); actual line BELOW ideal → team is ahead; FLAT PERIODS: the line doesn't drop → team is stuck (blockers, dependencies, or the sprint is overcommitted); SPRINT BURNDOWN vs. RELEASE BURNDOWN: sprint burndown: progress within a single 1-4 week sprint; release burndown: progress across multiple sprints toward a release goal; WHAT BURNDOWN REVEALS: whether the team will complete all committed work by sprint end; early warning of velocity problems; whether work is being added mid-sprint (line goes up instead of down).
explanations.b: A cost burn rate chart tracks financial spending — not work remaining. These are different charts measuring different dimensions. 'Burn' in burndown refers to work being completed (burned through), not money being spent.
explanations.c: Team member availability is shown in a resource calendar — not a burndown chart.
explanations.d: Defects remaining is shown on a defect trend chart or bug burndown (a specific type of burndown) — not a standard sprint burndown chart.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — network diagram; activity dependencies; critical path visualization
questions.text: A project manager creates a network diagram (also called a PERT chart in some contexts). What is the PRIMARY use of a network diagram?

answers.text: To visualize activity dependencies and calculate the critical path — showing which sequence of activities determines the project's minimum duration
To show team member hierarchy and reporting relationships
To show project budget allocation across cost centers
To display stakeholder power and interest levels

explanations.a: NETWORK DIAGRAM PRIMARY USE: shows ALL project activities and the DEPENDENCIES between them. KEY ELEMENTS: NODES: represent individual activities (work packages or tasks); ARROWS: represent dependencies (Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, Start-to-Finish); DIRECTION: activities flow from left to right (project start to project end); CRITICAL PATH: the longest sequence of dependent activities from project start to project end; determines the PROJECT'S MINIMUM DURATION; any delay on the critical path = the same delay to the project end date; FLOAT/SLACK: non-critical path activities have float — how many days they can slip before affecting the project end date; zero-float activities = on the critical path. NETWORK DIAGRAM vs. GANTT: NETWORK DIAGRAM: focuses on DEPENDENCIES and CRITICAL PATH; better for schedule analysis and 'what if' scenario planning; harder to read for non-PMs; GANTT CHART: focuses on TIMELINE and TASK DURATION; better for team communication; doesn't show critical path as clearly. TYPES: AOA (Activity on Arrow): activities represented by arrows; AON (Activity on Node): activities represented by boxes/nodes; AON is more common in modern PM tools. PRIMARY ANALYTICAL VALUE: calculating the critical path tells the PM which activities CANNOT SLIP without affecting the project delivery date — the most important scheduling insight.
explanations.b: Team member hierarchy and reporting relationships are shown in an organizational chart — not a network diagram.
explanations.c: Budget allocation is shown in cost breakdown or budget charts — not network diagrams.
explanations.d: Stakeholder power/interest is shown on a power-interest grid — not a network diagram.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — organizational chart; team structure; reporting relationships
questions.text: A project manager creates an organizational chart for a complex cross-functional project team. What does the organizational chart show and how is it useful during execution?

answers.text: The organizational chart shows team member roles, reporting relationships, and the structure of the project organization — who reports to whom; how work-streams are organized; how the project team relates to the broader organizational hierarchy
The organizational chart shows project activities plotted on a timeline
The organizational chart shows the percentage of budget spent by each team member
The organizational chart is identical to the RACI matrix — same tool, different name

explanations.a: ORGANIZATIONAL CHART (Org Chart) in project context: WHAT IT SHOWS: project team structure — roles, titles, and reporting relationships; hierarchical arrangement showing who reports to whom; functional group divisions within the project; contact for specific work-streams. FOR THE PROJECT TEAM (project org chart): project sponsor at top; project manager; work-stream leads; team members within each work-stream. FOR CROSS-FUNCTIONAL PROJECTS: shows how representatives from different departments are organized within the project structure; clarifies whether team members report to functional managers or to the project manager (functional vs. projectized vs. matrix structure). USES DURING EXECUTION: ONBOARDING: new team members quickly understand the team structure; STAKEHOLDER UNDERSTANDING: external stakeholders know who to contact for which work-stream; ESCALATION PATHS: shows the reporting chain for escalation purposes; VENDOR INTEGRATION: shows where vendor team members fit in the project structure. PROJECT ORG CHART vs. RACI MATRIX: org chart = who reports to whom (authority structure); RACI = who is Responsible/Accountable/Consulted/Informed for each deliverable (role assignment); they serve complementary but different purposes.
explanations.b: Activities on a timeline are shown in a Gantt chart — not an organizational chart.
explanations.c: Budget by team member is a resource cost report — not an organizational chart.
explanations.d: RACI and org charts serve different purposes: RACI shows work accountability for deliverables; org chart shows team structure and reporting relationships.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart; baseline vs. actual; schedule variance visualization
questions.text: A Gantt chart shows a project's current status. The 'baseline' bars (original plan) and 'actual' bars (current progress) are both visible. Activity 7 has a baseline end date of September 15 and its actual bar extends to September 22. Activity 12 shows the baseline bar shorter than the actual completion bar. What does each scenario indicate?

answers.text: Activity 7 is behind schedule (actual completion on September 22 is 7 days later than the September 15 baseline); Activity 12's actual completion extending beyond the baseline end date means Activity 12 took longer than planned (behind schedule or over-duration)
Activity 7 is ahead of schedule; Activity 12 is behind schedule
Both activities are on schedule — baseline and actual bars always appear different as a formatting choice
Activity 7 is exactly on schedule — September 22 is within the acceptable tolerance range of September 15

explanations.a: GANTT CHART BASELINE vs. ACTUAL INTERPRETATION: ACTIVITY 7 — SCHEDULE DELAY: BASELINE end date: September 15 (what was planned); ACTUAL end date: September 22 (when it actually completed or is currently projected to complete); September 22 > September 15 = 7 calendar days late; VISUAL: the actual bar EXTENDS BEYOND the right edge of the baseline bar; this extension represents the schedule variance (SV is negative for this activity); ACTIVITY 12 — DURATION OVERRUN: 'Actual bar shorter than actual completion bar' — if the actual bar extends beyond the baseline bar, the activity took more time than planned; the additional length of the actual bar beyond the baseline represents the additional time consumed; INTERPRETATION: Activity 12 is similarly delayed relative to its baseline. CRITICAL PATH CONSIDERATION: whether either delay affects the project end date depends on: whether the activity is on the critical path (zero float → any delay = project delay); whether the activity has remaining float (float absorbs the delay if float exceeds the variance). GANTT CHART VALUE for tracking: by overlaying baseline and actual, project managers and stakeholders can immediately see which activities are ahead, on track, or behind — no detailed schedule analysis required; RAG status can be derived from baseline vs. actual comparison.
explanations.b: An actual bar extending BEYOND the baseline indicates the activity took MORE time than planned — it is behind schedule, not ahead. An activity ahead of schedule would show the actual bar SHORTER than the baseline (completing early).
explanations.c: Baseline and actual bars showing different lengths and positions is meaningful — it shows schedule variance. If they appeared different purely for formatting, the baseline would be useless as a performance measurement tool.
explanations.d: 7 days late on September 15 baseline is a material schedule variance. Whether it's 'acceptable' depends on the activity's float and the project's schedule tolerance — but calling it 'on schedule' is incorrect.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — PERT chart; three-point estimating; expected duration formula
questions.text: A project manager uses PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) to estimate the duration of a complex software integration activity. The team provides three estimates: Optimistic (O) = 10 days, Most Likely (M) = 15 days, Pessimistic (P) = 28 days. Calculate the PERT expected duration and explain what makes PERT different from using only the 'most likely' estimate.

answers.text: PERT expected duration = (O + 4M + P) / 6 = (10 + 60 + 28) / 6 = 98/6 = 16.33 days; PERT weights the most likely estimate 4× to acknowledge it is more likely than the extremes; the expected duration (16.33) is higher than the most likely (15) because the pessimistic tail (28) pulls the weighted average up — PERT accounts for uncertainty and schedule risk more realistically than a single point estimate
PERT expected duration = (O + M + P) / 3 = (10+15+28)/3 = 17.67 days
PERT expected duration = P − O = 28 − 10 = 18 days (the range)
PERT uses only the pessimistic estimate — the pessimistic value provides the most conservative schedule

explanations.a: PERT FORMULA: Expected Duration = (O + 4M + P) / 6; CALCULATION: O = 10, M = 15, P = 28; = (10 + (4×15) + 28) / 6; = (10 + 60 + 28) / 6; = 98 / 6; = 16.33 days. WHY PERT vs. MOST LIKELY: PERT ACCOUNTS FOR ASYMMETRIC UNCERTAINTY: the most likely estimate (15 days) reflects the typical case; the pessimistic estimate (28 days) is 13 days above most likely; the optimistic estimate (10 days) is only 5 days below most likely; real-world project activities often have LONGER tails on the pessimistic side (things go wrong more often than they go wonderfully right); the PERT formula's weighting (4M + extremes ÷ 6) captures this asymmetry; EXPECTED VALUE: the PERT expected duration (16.33 days) is the AVERAGE OUTCOME across all probability-weighted scenarios; using 15 days (most likely) would underestimate duration in expectation because the pessimistic tail is heavier; PRACTICAL USE: schedule buffers derived from PERT estimates are more realistic than those derived from most-likely-only estimates; PERT is particularly valuable for: novel activities with high uncertainty; activities with complex dependencies; research or technical discovery work where the pessimistic scenario is meaningfully different from the most likely. STANDARD DEVIATION: σ = (P−O)/6 = (28−10)/6 = 3 days → provides the variability estimate for probabilistic schedule analysis.
explanations.b: The formula (O+M+P)/3 is a simple average — not the PERT formula. PERT specifically weights the most likely estimate 4× because it is more probable than the extremes.
explanations.c: P−O = 28−10 = 18 is the RANGE — a measure of uncertainty, not the expected duration.
explanations.d: Using only the pessimistic estimate would be overly conservative, producing schedules that almost always finish early — which is also not accurate.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — burndown chart; reading burndown; sprint health indicators
questions.text: A 10-day sprint burndown chart shows: Day 1: 50 points remaining (all sprint work); Days 2-4: remaining work stays at 50 (no decrease); Day 5: remaining work jumps to 60 (10 points added); Days 6-10: line descends from 60 to 15. What does this burndown pattern reveal?

answers.text: The sprint was completed successfully — any burndown ending with points remaining is normal
The Day 5 spike means the team completed extra work and added it to the sprint — the chart shows overcapacity

The burndown reveals three distinct patterns: Days 1-4 flat at 50 (blocked — no work completed for 3 days, a serious impediment needs investigation); Day 5 spike from 50 to 60 (scope was added mid-sprint — 10 story points added without removing equivalent work, potentially disrupting sprint commitment); Days 6-10 descent to 15 (team worked productively but the sprint ends with 15 points remaining — sprint goal not fully achieved)
The burndown is perfectly normal — all burndown charts look like this

explanations.a: A sprint ending with 15 story points remaining (out of 50 originally committed — 30% incomplete) is not 'normal.' The sprint goal was not met. The burndown pattern reveals multiple sprint health issues.
explanations.b: A line going UP in a burndown chart means work was ADDED (more remaining work), not completed. Completed work would cause the line to go DOWN.
explanations.c: BURNDOWN PATTERN ANALYSIS: DAYS 1-4 — FLAT LINE AT 50 POINTS (MAJOR CONCERN): zero work completed in the first 3 sprint days; CAUSES: blockers preventing work start (environment not set up, dependencies not available, unclear acceptance criteria); team members unavailable or working on non-sprint work; stories not properly refined for development to begin; SCRUM MASTER ACTION: in the Day 2 stand-up, the Scrum master should have identified the impediment immediately; a flat burndown for 3 days in a 10-day sprint means 30% of the sprint is gone without progress; DAY 5 SPIKE FROM 50 TO 60 — SCOPE ADDITION: remaining work INCREASES from 50 to 60 = 10 story points were added; this violates sprint integrity: once a sprint begins, the committed scope should remain fixed unless extraordinary circumstances warrant changes; the product owner added work without removing equivalent work; this further risks sprint goal achievement; DAYS 6-10 — DESCENT TO 15 REMAINING: the team worked productively (burning down 45 points in 5 days = 9 points/day); however, starting from 60 points with 5 days of productive work (9 points/day × 5 days = 45 points burned), 60−45=15 remaining is logical; SPRINT OUTCOME: 15 of 60 points incomplete (25% of work not delivered); the sprint goal was likely not met; retrospective should address: what caused the 3-day blockage?; why was scope added mid-sprint?; what will prevent recurrence?
explanations.d: This burndown pattern shows multiple sprint dysfunction signals — flat lines, scope additions, and incomplete delivery are not normal.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — network diagram; critical path calculation; float analysis
questions.text: A network diagram shows three paths through a project: Path A (Activities 1→2→5): 8+6+4 = 18 days. Path B (Activities 1→3→5): 8+9+4 = 21 days. Path C (Activities 1→4→5): 8+3+4 = 15 days. Which is the critical path and how much float does Path A have?

answers.text: Path A is the critical path (18 days); Path B and C have no float
All three paths are critical — every path is critical in a network diagram
Path B is the critical path (21 days — longest path); Path A has 3 days of float (21−18=3); Path C has 6 days of float (21−15=6); the project minimum duration is 21 days
Path C is the critical path (15 days — shortest path determines project duration)

explanations.a: The critical path is the LONGEST path — not just any path. Path B (21 days) is the longest and therefore the critical path.
explanations.b: Not all paths are critical — only the longest path(s) are critical. Activities on non-critical paths have positive float.
explanations.c: CRITICAL PATH CALCULATION: DEFINITION: the CRITICAL PATH is the LONGEST path through the network from start to finish; determines the project's MINIMUM possible duration (the project cannot finish in less than 21 days); CALCULATION: Path A: 8+6+4 = 18 days; Path B: 8+9+4 = 21 days (LONGEST = CRITICAL PATH); Path C: 8+3+4 = 15 days. PROJECT DURATION: 21 days (determined by Path B, the critical path). FLOAT CALCULATION: FLOAT (also called SLACK) = Longest path − Path duration; Path A float = 21 − 18 = 3 days; Path A can slip up to 3 days without affecting the project end date; Path C float = 21 − 15 = 6 days; Path C can slip up to 6 days without affecting the project end date; Path B float = 21 − 21 = 0 days; ANY delay on Path B DIRECTLY delays the project end date. MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS: the PM must closely monitor Activity 3 (Path B's unique activity) — it has no float; Activities 2 and 4 have float — they are not the PM's primary concern; if Activity 3 is delayed by 1 day, the project is delayed by 1 day. CRITICAL PATH vs. NEAR-CRITICAL: Path A with only 3 days of float is 'near-critical' — a small delay converts it to critical; the PM should monitor both Path B (critical) and Path A (near-critical) carefully.
explanations.d: The critical path is the LONGEST, not the SHORTEST. The shortest path has the MOST float — it can slip the most without affecting the project end date.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart; appropriate use cases; audience suitability
questions.text: A project manager has three communication needs: (1) Show the project team all 80 scheduled activities with durations, dependencies, and current completion status; (2) Show the steering committee which of 10 major milestones are on track, at risk, or delayed; (3) Show the development leads which sprint activities are in progress, complete, or blocked this week. Which chart type is MOST appropriate for each need?

answers.text: Use a network diagram for all three — it's the most comprehensive chart
Use a Gantt chart for all three — Gantt charts serve all schedule communication needs

(1) Gantt chart — the project team needs full task-level detail with durations, progress, and dependencies in a time-scaled format; (2) Milestone chart — the steering committee needs high-level status of key events without task-level detail; (3) Sprint-level Gantt or Kanban board — development leads need current sprint task status at a tactical level
Use a burndown chart for all three — burndown is the most modern schedule tracking tool

explanations.a: A network diagram is used for critical path analysis and dependency visualization — not for operational task tracking or executive milestone reporting.
explanations.b: While a Gantt chart CAN serve all three needs, it is not OPTIMAL for all three: a 200-task Gantt for a steering committee is overwhelming; the steering committee needs a milestone view; the development team during a sprint needs sprint-specific views.
explanations.c: CHART SELECTION BY AUDIENCE AND NEED: (1) PROJECT TEAM — ALL 80 ACTIVITIES: BEST CHART: Full Gantt Chart; WHY: shows all 80 activities with planned start/end dates; duration bars show relative length of each activity; dependency arrows show task relationships; percentage-complete bars show current progress; baselines overlay shows variance from plan; allows team members to see how their work connects to others; TOOL: MS Project, Smartsheet, Monday.com; (2) STEERING COMMITTEE — 10 MILESTONES: BEST CHART: Milestone Chart; WHY: executives need strategic visibility, not operational detail; 10 milestones fit on 1 page with RAG status; shows critical dates without overwhelming detail; enables 5-minute governance review instead of 2-hour schedule deep-dive; appropriate detail level matches the governance role; (3) DEVELOPMENT LEADS — CURRENT SPRINT: BEST CHART: Sprint-level Gantt OR Kanban Board; SPRINT GANTT: zoomed to the current sprint (2-week view); shows individual sprint stories/tasks with day-level detail; progress visible at task level; KANBAN BOARD: shows stories in 'To Do / In Progress / Done / Blocked' columns; visual representation of sprint state; immediate visibility into blockers; popular in Scrum teams for daily stand-up use. PRINCIPLE: the right chart matches the information need and the audience's decision-making level.
explanations.d: Burndown charts track remaining work over time — they are excellent for sprint progress but don't show task-level details for team coordination or milestone status for executives.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — PERT vs. network diagram; distinction and use cases
questions.text: A colleague says: 'PERT and network diagrams are the same thing.' The project manager needs to clarify the distinction. What is the ACCURATE relationship between PERT and network diagrams?

answers.text: They are identical — PERT and network diagram are different names for the same tool
Network diagrams replaced PERT — PERT is obsolete and no longer used in project management

PERT uses network diagrams as its visual representation, but PERT is the broader TECHNIQUE that includes three-point estimating (O, M, P) to calculate probabilistic durations; a network diagram is simply the diagram that shows activity dependencies and sequence — it can be used with or without PERT estimating
PERT is only for Agile projects; network diagrams are only for Waterfall projects

explanations.a: PERT and network diagrams are related but distinct: a network diagram is the VISUAL REPRESENTATION that PERT uses, but a network diagram can exist without PERT estimating, and PERT's primary contribution is the three-point estimating formula — not the diagram itself.
explanations.b: PERT remains a valid and useful technique for projects with high duration uncertainty. The three-point estimating formula is still taught and applied in project management.
explanations.c: PERT vs. NETWORK DIAGRAM CLARIFICATION: NETWORK DIAGRAM: a VISUAL TOOL showing project activities as nodes and dependencies as arrows; shows the sequence and relationships between activities; used to calculate the critical path (CPM — Critical Path Method); can use single-point duration estimates; the DIAGRAM is the visual representation. PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique): a TECHNIQUE developed for the US Navy Polaris missile program in the 1950s; PERT's key contribution: THREE-POINT ESTIMATING (Optimistic, Most Likely, Pessimistic) to handle duration uncertainty; PERT EXPECTED DURATION formula: (O + 4M + P) / 6; PERT uses a NETWORK DIAGRAM as its visual representation; PERT typically refers to the combination of: network diagram for dependency sequencing + probabilistic three-point estimating for duration uncertainty. WHEN TO USE EACH: Use a NETWORK DIAGRAM alone (with CPM): when you have reliable single-point estimates; for construction, manufacturing, and well-understood project types; Use PERT specifically: when durations are highly uncertain; when probabilistic scheduling is needed; novel or research-oriented projects with unknown territory. MODERN USAGE: modern project management software (MS Project, Primavera) uses network diagrams for CPM calculation and can apply PERT estimating — the two are often used together but are conceptually distinct.
explanations.d: PERT originated in traditional/Waterfall project management (1950s Navy program); network diagrams are used in both Waterfall and some Agile scaling frameworks.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — burndown vs. burnup chart; scope change visibility; release tracking
questions.text: A product owner asks whether the team should use a BURNDOWN chart or a BURNUP chart for release tracking when scope frequently changes. What is the DIFFERENCE and which is better for this situation?

answers.text: Burndown and burnup charts are identical — they display the same information
Burndown is always better — it shows how much work is left more clearly than burnup
Burnup is only for Waterfall projects; burndown is only for Agile projects

Burndown shows REMAINING work (decreasing toward zero); burnup shows COMPLETED work (increasing toward the total scope line); when scope changes frequently, burnup is BETTER because it shows both completed work AND total scope on the same chart — scope additions cause the total scope line to rise, making scope changes visible without disrupting the completed-work line

explanations.a: Burndown and burnup display fundamentally different things: one shows remaining work (going down), the other shows completed work (going up). They provide different insights about scope and progress.
explanations.b: Burndown is simpler and sufficient for stable-scope sprints. For release-level tracking with frequent scope changes, burnup provides clearer visibility of all dimensions.
explanations.c: Both charts are used in Agile projects; both can be adapted for Waterfall phases. The choice is based on information visibility needs, not methodology.
explanations.d: BURNDOWN vs. BURNUP COMPARISON: BURNDOWN CHART: Y-axis: REMAINING work (story points, hours); starts HIGH and burns DOWN toward zero; goal: reach zero at sprint/release end; SCOPE CHANGE PROBLEM: when scope is added mid-sprint, remaining work INCREASES (line goes up) — this looks the same as work not being completed; the burndown chart cannot distinguish between 'team is behind' and 'scope was added' without additional annotation. BURNUP CHART: Y-axis: COMPLETED work (story points, hours); starts at ZERO and burns UP toward the total scope; two lines: (1) COMPLETED WORK line: moves upward as work is done; (2) TOTAL SCOPE line: a horizontal target line showing total committed scope; SCOPE CHANGE VISIBILITY: when scope is added, the TOTAL SCOPE line moves up; when scope is removed, the TOTAL SCOPE line moves down; the completed work line continues its upward progress independent of scope changes; the GAP between the two lines shows remaining work at any point. FOR FREQUENTLY CHANGING SCOPE: BURNUP IS BETTER because: scope changes are clearly visible as movements in the total scope line; stakeholders can see: how much has been completed; how scope has changed; whether the team is making progress toward the (changing) target; progress is not artificially distorted by scope additions; a burndown where scope changes are hidden would create confusion about whether slowdowns are team performance or scope additions.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart; status reporting; progress tracking mechanics
questions.text: A project manager updates the Gantt chart weekly. For Activity 15 (planned 10 days, started on the planned date), by Day 6 the activity shows 40% complete. The planned completion date was Day 10. Is this activity on track and how should the Gantt reflect this?

answers.text: The activity is on track — 40% complete by Day 6 is exactly right
Progress cannot be assessed until the activity is 100% complete — measuring mid-activity progress is unreliable
40% complete by Day 6 is excellent — the activity is ahead of schedule

The activity is BEHIND schedule: by Day 6 of a 10-day activity, 60% should be complete (6/10 = 60%); actual 40% complete = 20% behind planned progress; Gantt should show: the progress bar shaded to 40% of the bar length; the Gantt's 'percent complete' line should stop at the Day 6 mark, showing the gap between where completion should be (60%) and where it is (40%); this may also be reflected as a schedule variance in EVM (EV < PV)

explanations.a: By Day 6 of a 10-day activity, if progress were perfectly linear, 60% should be complete (6 days ÷ 10 days = 60%). Only 40% complete represents a 20-percentage-point gap — the activity is behind planned progress.
explanations.b: Mid-activity progress measurement is essential for early warning of schedule problems. If 'you can't measure progress until completion,' late discovery of problems is guaranteed — exactly what progress tracking is designed to prevent.
explanations.c: 40% complete by Day 6 when 60% was planned is NOT ahead of schedule — it is 20 percentage points behind planned progress.
explanations.d: GANTT CHART PROGRESS TRACKING: PLANNED PROGRESS by Day 6: 6 days elapsed / 10 planned days = 60% planned complete (assuming linear progress); ACTUAL PROGRESS: 40% complete; VARIANCE: 40% actual − 60% planned = −20% (behind plan); GANTT REPRESENTATION: PROGRESS BAR: the horizontal bar for Activity 15 is 10 units wide (representing 10 days); the shaded completion portion covers only 40% of the bar width (4 units of 10); the 'today' line (vertical marker for the current date) is at Day 6; the progress bar ends at the 40% mark, which is to the LEFT of the 'today' line — visually showing the activity is behind; SCHEDULE SLIP CALCULATION: if the remaining 60% of work proceeds at 40%/6 days = 6.67%/day rate: 60% remaining / 6.67%/day = 9 more days to complete; projected total duration: 6 + 9 = 15 days vs. 10-day plan = 5 days late; if the team can accelerate back to the expected rate (6%/day): 60% remaining / 6%/day = 10 more days; projected total duration: 6 + 10 = 16 days — still late; PM ACTION: investigate the reason for the 20% progress gap; determine if recovery is possible (additional resources, overtime, simplified approach).

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — network diagram; reading dependencies; lag and lead time
questions.text: A network diagram shows the following: Activity A (5 days) → [FS + 2 days lag] → Activity B (8 days). Activity A (5 days) → [SS + 1 day lead] → Activity C (6 days). What do the lag and lead time designations mean and when would each be appropriate?

answers.text: Lag and lead time are the same thing — they are interchangeable terms
Lag is added to pessimistic estimates; lead is added to optimistic estimates — both are PERT estimation adjustments
Lag means the activity is behind schedule; lead means the activity is ahead of schedule — both are performance indicators

LAG (FS + 2 days): after Activity A finishes, there is a mandatory 2-day WAIT before Activity B can start (delay added to the dependency); LAG example: concrete must cure for 2 days before electrical work can begin. LEAD (SS + 1 day): Activity C can start 1 day BEFORE Activity A finishes (overlap of sequential activities); LEAD example: documentation can begin 1 day before development finishes, giving documentation a head start

explanations.a: Lag and lead are opposite concepts: lag ADDS waiting time (delays the dependent activity); lead REDUCES waiting time (allows overlap with the predecessor).
explanations.b: Lag and lead are dependency relationship modifiers — not estimation adjustments for PERT.
explanations.c: Lag and lead are schedule PLANNING tools — they define dependency relationships between activities, not performance status.
explanations.d: LAG TIME: adds a mandatory waiting period BETWEEN the predecessor and successor; NOTATION: FS + 2 days = Finish-to-Start with 2 days of lag; meaning: wait 2 days after A finishes before B can start; APPROPRIATE WHEN: physical or regulatory requirements mandate a waiting period (concrete curing; paint drying; document review period; regulatory approval processing time; environmental monitoring window); EFFECT ON SCHEDULE: increases the overall project duration (a 2-day lag adds 2 days to the path duration). LEAD TIME (also called negative lag): allows a successor activity to start BEFORE its predecessor finishes; NOTATION: SS + 1 day = Start-to-Start with 1 day of lead; or sometimes expressed as FS − 1 = Finish-to-Start with 1 day of lead (negative lag); meaning: Activity C starts 1 day AFTER Activity A starts (not waiting for A to finish); APPROPRIATE WHEN: the successor doesn't need ALL of the predecessor's output to begin; documentation can start before the last module of development finishes; testing can begin on completed components before the final component is done; SCHEDULE COMPRESSION: lead time enables fast-tracking — allowing overlap between activities that were originally sequential, compressing the overall schedule; RISK: if Activity A changes significantly after Activity C has already started based on A's early output, C may require rework.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — milestone chart; selecting appropriate milestones; milestone criteria
questions.text: A project manager is building a milestone chart for a 12-month ERP implementation. From the 200-task project schedule, she must select 8-10 milestones. What criteria should guide milestone selection?

answers.text: Select the 8-10 most time-consuming activities — duration determines milestone importance
Select the 8-10 most recent activities — recency makes milestones relevant
Select the first 8-10 activities in the schedule — milestones should be in chronological order from the beginning only

Select events that: (1) represent a significant project state change or phase completion (requirements baseline approved; UAT start; go-live); (2) are dependencies for major downstream work; (3) serve as natural decision or review points (steering committee decision points); (4) represent contractual or regulatory obligations; (5) indicate points where the stakeholder can verify project direction — these are governance checkpoints, not just arbitrary points in time

explanations.a: Duration determines task scope, not governance importance. A 5-day critical decision has more milestone value than a 30-day non-critical activity.
explanations.b: Recency does not determine milestone importance. The go-live milestone (the most important milestone for stakeholders) may be 9 months away — but it belongs in the milestone chart.
explanations.c: Including only the first 8-10 chronological activities creates a milestone chart that's useful only in the first month — it provides no visibility into the project's overall trajectory and critical future events.
explanations.d: MILESTONE SELECTION CRITERIA: PHASE COMPLETIONS: Requirements Complete; Design Approved; Development Complete; UAT Complete; Go-Live; these represent transitions between major project phases where the work fundamentally changes; DEPENDENCIES FOR DOWNSTREAM WORK: any milestone whose completion is a prerequisite for major subsequent work; if the architecture review is not complete, development cannot begin — this is a milestone; DECISION POINTS: points where the steering committee decides to continue, modify, or stop the project; phase gate decisions; go/no-go reviews; these are governance checkpoints that belong on every milestone chart; CONTRACTUAL/REGULATORY MILESTONES: delivery of contractually committed deliverables; regulatory submission or approval dates; legal compliance deadlines; these have external accountability and must be tracked visibly; MEANINGFUL STATE CHANGES: not just activity completions, but moments when the project's state meaningfully changes from the stakeholder's perspective; 'System Integration Testing Begins' marks the transition from development to verification; EXAMPLES for ERP: (1) Business Requirements Baseline Signed; (2) Technical Architecture Approved; (3) Development Sprint 1 Complete (MVP delivered to UAT); (4) Vendor Integration Testing Complete; (5) User Acceptance Testing Start; (6) UAT Formal Acceptance; (7) Security Review Approved; (8) Go-Live; (9) 30-Day Post Go-Live Stability Review; (10) Project Closure.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — organizational chart; project org chart types; matrix vs. projectized structure
questions.text: A project uses a matrix organizational structure where team members report to BOTH a functional manager and the project manager. How should the project org chart represent this dual-reporting reality, and what conflicts can this create?

answers.text: The project org chart should show only the project manager hierarchy — functional reporting is irrelevant
In a matrix structure, the project manager has no authority over team members — the org chart shows only functional reporting
Matrix structures are too complex to show in an org chart — verbal description is sufficient

A matrix org chart explicitly shows dual reporting lines: solid lines represent the primary reporting relationship (typically to the functional manager for administrative matters — HR, performance review, salary); dotted lines represent the secondary reporting relationship (to the project manager for project work priorities); the dual-reporting structure can create conflicts when functional manager priorities and project manager priorities compete for the same person's time

explanations.a: A project org chart that ignores functional reporting misrepresents the authority structure and can create confusion about who has priority when both managers make competing demands.
explanations.b: In a matrix structure, the project manager DOES have authority over team members regarding project work — this is exactly what distinguishes a matrix from a pure functional structure. The authority is SHARED between PM and functional manager, not exclusively with the functional manager.
explanations.c: Matrix structures can be clearly represented in org charts — dual reporting lines (solid + dotted) are a standard notation used precisely to show this structure.
explanations.d: MATRIX ORG CHART REPRESENTATION: SOLID LINE (administrative authority): shows the functional manager → team member relationship; functional manager handles: performance reviews; salary decisions; vacation approval; HR issues; career development; DOTTED LINE (project authority): shows the project manager → team member relationship; project manager controls: day-to-day work priorities; task assignments; quality standards; delivery timelines; project reporting requirements; VISUAL: a team member in a matrix appears in TWO places: under their functional manager (solid line); under the project manager (dotted line). CONFLICTS IN MATRIX STRUCTURES: TIME ALLOCATION CONFLICTS: functional manager wants team member on a new department initiative; project manager needs them for a critical path activity; the team member is caught in the middle — who takes priority?; RESOLUTION: typically requires escalation to a common superior; some organizations have PMO priority rules; PERFORMANCE REVIEW CONFLICTS: functional manager evaluates performance; but project manager knows 80% of the employee's actual work quality; best practice: PM provides input to functional manager's review; AUTHORITY AMBIGUITY: team members may be uncertain whose instruction to follow when priorities conflict; clear role definitions in the RACI matrix help reduce this confusion. MATRIX VARIANTS: WEAK MATRIX: functional manager has more authority; PM acts more as a coordinator; BALANCED MATRIX: shared authority; STRONG MATRIX: PM has more authority; closer to projectized structure.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — selecting the right chart; multiple stakeholder needs; chart comparison
questions.text: A PM needs to address four specific information needs: (1) Determine which activities have zero float and cannot slip without delaying the project; (2) Show a CFO the project's top 8 completion events with their current status in a 1-page format; (3) Show the Agile development team how much work remains in the current 2-week sprint; (4) Show the project team the complete schedule with all 60 tasks, their sequence, progress, and duration. Map the BEST chart type for each need.

answers.text: Use a Gantt chart for all four — Gantt charts address all scheduling needs
(1) Burndown chart; (2) Gantt chart; (3) Network diagram; (4) Milestone chart
(1) Milestone chart; (2) Network diagram; (3) Gantt chart; (4) Burndown chart

(1) Network diagram with CPM — identifies critical path (zero-float activities); (2) Milestone chart — 8 key events in 1-page executive format; (3) Burndown chart — remaining sprint work tracked day by day; (4) Gantt chart — complete schedule with all 60 tasks, durations, and progress

explanations.a: A Gantt chart can show task sequence and some dependency information, but it does not directly show which activities have zero float (that requires CPM calculation, which is visualized in the network diagram or CPM analysis). Using Gantt for all four needs would produce suboptimal communication for three of the four needs.
explanations.b: This answer has all four charts mismatched to their needs.
explanations.c: This answer mismatches charts to needs: a milestone chart cannot determine which activities have zero float (requires CPM); a network diagram doesn't provide an executive 1-page view; a Gantt doesn't show sprint remaining work as simply as a burndown; a burndown doesn't communicate 60-task complete schedule.
explanations.d: CHART SELECTION — BEST FIT ANALYSIS: (1) ZERO-FLOAT ACTIVITIES → NETWORK DIAGRAM with CPM: the critical path method (CPM) uses a network diagram to calculate: Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF) for each activity; Float = LS − ES (or LF − EF); zero-float activities = critical path = cannot slip; a Gantt chart can SHOW the critical path after calculation, but the CALCULATION itself uses the network diagram's dependency structure; if the question is 'which activities have zero float,' the analytical tool is CPM via the network diagram. (2) CFO — 8 COMPLETION EVENTS, 1-PAGE → MILESTONE CHART: a milestone chart with 8 milestones and RAG status is exactly what a CFO needs: fits on 1 page; shows strategic-level events; quick RAG assessment; no operational detail that an executive doesn't need. (3) AGILE TEAM — SPRINT REMAINING WORK → BURNDOWN CHART: shows story points remaining vs. ideal burndown line; team can see sprint health at a glance; updated daily; triggers early discussion of blockers when actual line diverges from ideal. (4) PROJECT TEAM — 60 TASKS WITH SEQUENCE AND PROGRESS → GANTT CHART: shows all 60 tasks in sequence; horizontal bars with duration; dependency arrows; progress bars showing % complete; baseline vs. actual overlay; exactly designed for this comprehensive team-level schedule communication.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart limitations; when to use other chart types
questions.text: A project manager who relies exclusively on Gantt charts is asked: 'How do you know which tasks you MUST protect from slipping?' and 'What is the probability that the project will finish by the planned date?' The PM cannot answer either question from the Gantt alone. What additional tools address each question?

answers.text: Both questions can be answered from a Gantt chart with enough detail — the PM just needs a better Gantt
Both questions are impossible to answer — schedule uncertainty is inherent and unquantifiable
(1) Use a burndown chart to find critical tasks; (2) Use a milestone chart for probability analysis

(1) 'Which tasks must be protected from slipping?' is answered by CPM via a NETWORK DIAGRAM — identifying the critical path (zero-float activities); (2) 'Probability of finishing by the planned date?' is answered by PERT (probabilistic duration estimates producing a probability distribution for project completion) or Monte Carlo simulation

explanations.a: A standard Gantt chart does not inherently show which activities have zero float (unless CPM calculations are explicitly integrated). Modern project management software (MS Project) can calculate and display the critical path, but the underlying calculation is CPM — the Gantt is just the display format. The probability question requires statistical methods beyond what a standard Gantt provides.
explanations.b: Schedule uncertainty IS quantifiable using PERT and Monte Carlo simulation — these are established techniques for exactly this purpose.
explanations.c: Burndown charts show sprint/release remaining work — not critical path identification. Milestone charts show key events — not probability analysis.
explanations.d: GANTT CHART LIMITATIONS AND SUPPLEMENTARY TOOLS: (1) 'WHICH TASKS MUST BE PROTECTED FROM SLIPPING?' LIMITATION: a standard Gantt chart shows all activities as bars of various lengths; it does not inherently show which activities have float and which have zero float unless CPM analysis is specifically added; SOLUTION — CPM via NETWORK DIAGRAM: Critical Path Method (CPM) calculates forward pass (Early Start, Early Finish) and backward pass (Late Start, Late Finish) for each activity; Float = Late Start − Early Start; zero-float activities = critical path = MUST be protected from slipping; this is the fundamental analytical question the network diagram/CPM is designed to answer. (2) 'PROBABILITY OF FINISHING BY PLANNED DATE?' LIMITATION: a Gantt chart shows a deterministic schedule — each activity has one planned duration; it cannot show the probability distribution of completion dates; SOLUTION — PERT OR MONTE CARLO SIMULATION: PERT: each activity's duration is uncertain; three-point estimates (O, M, P) define the distribution; PERT provides a statistical completion date distribution; MONTE CARLO SIMULATION: runs thousands of random scenarios (each activity duration randomly selected from its probability distribution); produces a histogram showing: probability of finishing by a given date; percentile-based completion date forecasts; example output: '80% probability of completing by September 30; 50% probability by September 15'.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — organizational chart; project team structure design; governance clarity
questions.text: A project manager is designing the project org chart for a $3M cloud migration project with: a sponsor, a project manager, three work-stream leads (Infrastructure, Security, Application), each leading teams of 3-4 people, an external cloud vendor team (5 members), and a part-time PMO coordinator. How should the org chart be structured?

answers.text: List all 20 team members alphabetically — alphabetical is the most objective structure

Structure by reporting hierarchy: Sponsor at top; PM reporting to Sponsor; three Work-Stream Leads reporting to PM; team members reporting to their respective leads; PMO coordinator reporting to PM; external vendor team shown in a separate box with a dotted line to the PM (contractual relationship, not direct report); clearly labeled roles indicate internal vs. vendor staff
Exclude the vendor team — only internal employees appear in project org charts
Put all team members reporting directly to the sponsor — flat hierarchies are most efficient

explanations.a: Alphabetical listing shows who is on the project — but provides no information about team structure, reporting relationships, work-stream organization, or authority lines. An alphabetical list is a contact directory, not an organizational chart.
explanations.b: PROJECT ORG CHART DESIGN for the cloud migration: HIERARCHY STRUCTURE: LEVEL 1 — SPONSOR: executive authority; approves major decisions; chairs steering committee; LEVEL 2 — PROJECT MANAGER: overall project accountability; reports to sponsor; LEVEL 3 — WORK-STREAM LEADS (3): Infrastructure Lead; Security Lead; Application Lead; each reports directly to PM; PMO Coordinator (dotted or solid line to PM, depending on authority level); LEVEL 4 — TEAM MEMBERS (9-12): 3-4 team members under each work-stream lead; each team member reports to their respective lead; VENDOR TEAM REPRESENTATION: shown in a SEPARATE BOX (indicating a different organizational entity); DOTTED LINE to PM: the vendor team's PM communicates with and is governed by the project PM; dotted line = contractual/collaborative relationship (not direct employment); the vendor box clearly labeled 'Vendor — [Company Name]'; 5 vendor team members shown within the vendor box; INTERNAL vs. VENDOR DISTINCTION: clear visual differentiation (different color/shading for vendor box); GOVERNANCE CLARITY: the org chart immediately shows: who the PM manages directly (3 work-stream leads + PMO coordinator); who the PM governs contractually (vendor PM); who the sponsor should engage (PM, not work-stream leads directly); escalation paths (team member → work-stream lead → PM → sponsor).
explanations.c: Vendor teams are an integral part of the project team — their inclusion in the org chart (with appropriate notation as a dotted-line/contractual relationship) is standard practice and prevents confusion about governance.
explanations.d: All 20 team members reporting directly to the sponsor creates an unmanageable 20-person span of control for the sponsor and eliminates the project manager's governance role.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — milestone chart; RAG status assignment; milestone reporting
questions.text: A milestone chart shows 8 milestones. The PM must assign RAG status to each. Milestone 3 (Requirements Complete) was due May 1 and was completed May 5 — 4 days late. Milestone 5 (Architecture Review) is due June 15 and currently has no known risks. Milestone 7 (UAT Start) is due August 1 but a vendor delay (2 weeks behind) threatens this milestone with no recovery plan yet. How should each be categorized?

answers.text: All three milestones are Red — any issue makes a milestone Red
All three milestones are Green — past delays don't affect current status

Milestone 3 (completed 4 days late): Gray or historical — it is complete; the delay should be noted in the variance column; current status = complete (not Red anymore since it's done). Milestone 5 (due June 15, no risks): Green — on track, no identified risks. Milestone 7 (threatened by vendor 2-week delay, no recovery plan): Red — a known risk is actively threatening this milestone with no mitigation plan; action required
Milestone 3: Amber; Milestone 5: Red; Milestone 7: Green — invert the colors for dramatic effect

explanations.a: Assigning all milestones Red regardless of status makes the milestone chart useless as a decision tool — if everything is Red, executives cannot identify which milestones need their attention.
explanations.b: Ignoring Milestone 7's threat because it's 'not yet late' misrepresents project health. The purpose of milestone reporting is early warning — by the time Milestone 7 is actually late, it may be too late to take corrective action.
explanations.c: MILESTONE RAG STATUS ASSIGNMENT: MILESTONE 3 (Requirements Complete — COMPLETED 4 days late): CURRENT STATUS: COMPLETE (shows as Gray/checked/historical); the delay (4 days) should be documented in a 'variance' column for the record; RAG assignment is no longer relevant for a completed milestone — it's done; NOTE IN REPORT: 'M3 completed 4 days behind plan. Root cause: scope clarification workshop required an additional session. Impact: absorbed by planning phase float. No current impact on subsequent milestones.'; MILESTONE 5 (Architecture Review — due June 15, no known risks): CURRENT STATUS: GREEN; no risks identified; prerequisites are being completed on schedule; GREEN criteria: on track; no identified risks; MILESTONE 7 (UAT Start — threatened by vendor 2-week delay, no recovery): CURRENT STATUS: RED; a KNOWN risk exists (vendor 2 weeks behind) that will directly delay UAT Start; the delay creates a 2-week slip on August 1 = UAT now projected August 15; no recovery plan = no mitigation; RED criteria: milestone is threatened; delay is likely or confirmed; no mitigation plan in place; action required from the PM (and possibly sponsor); AMBER CRITERIA: risk exists but recovery is possible; a mitigation plan exists and is being executed; typically means 'watch closely' rather than 'take immediate action'; PRINCIPLE: RAG status reflects FORWARD-LOOKING RISK (what will happen) more than backward-looking performance (what did happen).
explanations.d: Inverting colors for 'dramatic effect' defeats the purpose of RAG status — executives rely on the universally understood Red=Problem/Green=OK convention for rapid status assessment.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt vs. Kanban board; Agile task tracking; visual management
questions.text: An Agile Scrum team is debating whether to use a Gantt chart or a Kanban board for their sprint task tracking. A team lead argues: 'We should use Gantt — it shows tasks with dates.' The Scrum master responds that a Kanban board is better for sprint execution. Who is correct and why?

answers.text: The team lead is correct — Gantt charts are always superior for task tracking

The Scrum master is correct for SPRINT EXECUTION tracking: a Kanban board (To Do / In Progress / Done columns) shows the CURRENT STATE of sprint stories visually and immediately; team members can update it in seconds; it's visible to the whole team during the daily stand-up; it shows blockers clearly; Gantt charts are better for RELEASE and PROJECT-level planning, not sprint-level day-to-day execution
Both tools are identical — the choice doesn't matter for sprint tracking
Neither tool works for Agile — Agile teams should only use burndown charts

explanations.a: Gantt charts have specific strengths (timeline-based, duration-focused, dependency visualization) and weaknesses (less effective for rapid, daily status updates in short iterations). For sprint execution, Kanban boards are better suited.
explanations.b: KANBAN vs. GANTT for SPRINT EXECUTION: KANBAN BOARD for sprint task tracking: VISUAL STATE REPRESENTATION: columns show task states: To Do | In Progress | Done | Blocked; each sprint story or task appears as a card in the appropriate column; IMMEDIATE UPDATE: team member moves their card from 'In Progress' to 'Done' in real time — no date calculations; DAILY STAND-UP TOOL: the Kanban board is the centerpiece of the daily stand-up: 'What did I move to Done yesterday? What am I working on In Progress today? What is Blocked?'; BLOCKER VISIBILITY: a 'Blocked' column or red sticker immediately shows which stories cannot progress; SPRINT HEALTH AT A GLANCE: if 8 stories are in 'To Do' with 3 days remaining, the team can see at a glance they need to triage; GANTT CHART for sprint use: NOT OPTIMAL for daily sprint execution because: adding precise dates to 1-2 week sprint stories is unnecessary overhead; daily updates to a Gantt chart are administratively heavy; the daily stand-up question is 'what's the status?' (current state) not 'when will it finish?' (date-based); HOWEVER — GANTT IS BETTER FOR: release planning (when will features be delivered across multiple sprints?); cross-team dependency visualization; project-level milestone tracking; SYNTHESIS: use both at different levels: KANBAN: sprint-level daily execution; GANTT: release-level and project-level planning; BURNDOWN: sprint velocity and remaining work tracking.
explanations.c: The choice of tracking tool significantly affects team communication efficiency, visibility of problems, and daily meeting effectiveness.
explanations.d: Agile teams use multiple chart types for different purposes: Kanban for sprint execution, burndown for sprint progress, release Gantt or roadmap for release planning.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — network diagram; critical path; schedule management using CPM
questions.text: During project execution, the network diagram shows the critical path running through Activities B→D→F→H. Activity D (on the critical path) is now 5 days behind schedule. Activity G (off the critical path, parallel to D, with 8 days of float) is still on schedule. How does this situation affect the project end date and what should the PM do?

answers.text: Activity G's on-schedule status compensates for Activity D's delay — the project remains on schedule

Activity D's 5-day delay on the critical path adds 5 days to the project end date; Activity G's float (8 days) is irrelevant to compensating for D's delay — float only applies to the specific activity that has it; the PM must focus recovery efforts on the critical path (D→F→H) through fast-tracking, crashing, or resource reallocation; G's on-schedule status is good news but provides no relief for the critical path delay
Since Activity G is on schedule, the critical path has shifted — G is now the critical path and D's delay doesn't matter
Activity D's delay only affects Activity D itself — other activities on the critical path are unaffected

explanations.a: Activity G's float does not compensate for Activity D's delay — they are on different paths. Float is path-specific: G has 8 days of float on its path; D has 0 float on the critical path. These are completely independent.
explanations.b: CRITICAL PATH DELAY ANALYSIS: ACTIVITY D (CRITICAL PATH — 5 DAYS LATE): the critical path is B→D→F→H; D is directly on this path with zero float; any delay in D propagates to all subsequent critical path activities: D's 5-day delay → F starts 5 days later → H starts 5 days later → project ends 5 days later; PROJECT IMPACT: project end date moves right by 5 days; ACTIVITY G (OFF CRITICAL PATH — ON SCHEDULE): G is parallel to D and not on the critical path; G has 8 days of float; G's on-schedule status is GOOD NEWS (it's not creating additional problems) but has NO BEARING on D's critical path delay; float is a buffer for the SPECIFIC ACTIVITY that has it — it doesn't transfer to other paths; CRITICAL PATH RECOVERY OPTIONS (what the PM should do): FAST-TRACKING: can Activities F or H begin before D is completely finished? If yes, overlap them with D to recover some time; CRASHING: add resources to Activity D to complete the remaining work faster; if D has 10 days of work remaining, adding a second person (if the work is parallelizable) might reduce it to 7-8 days; RESOURCE REALLOCATION: if G has idle capacity (it has 8 days of float and is on schedule), could G's resources temporarily assist D? This is an excellent reallocation strategy when activities share skill types. PRINCIPLE: the critical path defines the project end date; off-critical-path activities' performance cannot improve or offset critical path delays.
explanations.c: The critical path doesn't simply 'shift' to G because D is delayed. G would only become critical if its float was consumed — currently G has 8 days of float, so even with D's 5-day delay, G's 8 days of float means G can absorb up to 8 days before it becomes critical.
explanations.d: Activity D's delay on the critical path propagates to all subsequent critical path activities (F and H). Delays on the critical path are the definition of project-level schedule impact.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — burndown chart; release burndown; multi-sprint tracking
questions.text: A product owner is using a RELEASE burndown chart across 6 sprints (each sprint = 2 weeks). The release started with 360 story points. After Sprint 3, remaining work shows 220 points. Is the release on track and what does the release burndown reveal?

answers.text: The release is ahead of schedule — 220 points remaining after 3 sprints is excellent

After 3 of 6 sprints (50% of time elapsed), 220 of 360 points remain (61% remaining, not 50%); the release is BEHIND SCHEDULE pace; at the current velocity (140 points in 3 sprints = 46.7 points/sprint), 220 ÷ 46.7 = 4.7 more sprints needed; but only 3 sprints remain; at current velocity, the release will take 7.7 sprints total vs. the planned 6 — approximately 1.7 sprints late
Release burndown charts cannot be used for multi-sprint tracking — they are sprint-only tools
The release is exactly on track — 220 points remaining halfway through is normal

explanations.a: With 50% of sprints elapsed, 50% of story points should ideally be complete (180 points done). Actual: only 140 points done (39%) — meaning 61% of story points remain after 50% of scheduled time. This is behind pace, not ahead.
explanations.b: RELEASE BURNDOWN ANALYSIS: INITIAL STATE: 360 story points; 6 sprints planned; ACTUAL VELOCITY: Sprint 1-3 completed: 360 − 220 = 140 points; Average velocity: 140 / 3 = 46.7 points per sprint; PLANNED VELOCITY: to burn down 360 points in 6 sprints: 360 / 6 = 60 points/sprint planned; VARIANCE: actual 46.7 points/sprint vs. planned 60 points/sprint = 22% below planned velocity; STATUS ASSESSMENT: at Sprint 3 (50% of time): PLANNED remaining: 180 points (360 − 180 = 180 at 60/sprint × 3 sprints); ACTUAL remaining: 220 points; GAP: 40 points more remaining than planned (22% behind planned progress); FORECAST: remaining work: 220 points; remaining sprints: 3; FORECAST to complete all 220 points at 46.7 points/sprint: 220 / 46.7 = 4.7 sprints; but only 3 sprints remain; PROJECTED SHORTFALL: 4.7 − 3 = 1.7 sprints worth of work will not be delivered; RELEASE BURNDOWN REVEALS: (1) the team's average velocity is below the planned velocity required to meet the release date; (2) at current pace, approximately 76-77 story points will remain at Sprint 6 (3 sprints × 46.7 = 140 more burned; 220 − 140 = 80 remaining). PM/PO ACTIONS: reduce release scope (remove 80 lowest-priority points from the release backlog); increase velocity (if possible through process improvement, reduced interruptions); extend the release by 1-2 sprints (if timeline is negotiable).
explanations.c: Release burndown charts are designed SPECIFICALLY for multi-sprint tracking — they show progress toward a release goal across multiple sprints, making them essential for release planning and monitoring.
explanations.d: 220 points remaining with 50% of time elapsed when 61% of points are not yet done is clearly behind schedule — not 'exactly on track.'

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — PERT; standard deviation; schedule risk quantification
questions.text: A project has three sequential activities with these PERT estimates: Activity X (O=3, M=5, P=9); Activity Y (O=2, M=4, P=6); Activity Z (O=1, M=3, P=7). Calculate the total expected duration, total standard deviation, and explain what these numbers tell the PM about schedule risk.

answers.text: Total expected duration = sum of most likely estimates (5+4+3=12 days)

Activity X: E=(3+20+9)/6=32/6=5.33d, σ=(9-3)/6=1.00d; Activity Y: E=(2+16+6)/6=24/6=4.00d, σ=(6-2)/6=0.67d; Activity Z: E=(1+12+7)/6=20/6=3.33d, σ=(7-1)/6=1.00d; Total expected duration=12.67d; Total standard deviation=√(1.00²+0.67²+1.00²)=√(1+0.44+1)=√2.44=1.56 days; this means: expected completion is 12.67 days; there is approximately 68% probability of finishing between 11.11 and 14.23 days (±1 SD)
PERT standard deviation cannot be calculated without a computer — manual calculation is not possible
Standard deviation = (P-O)/6 for the project = (total P - total O)/6 = (9+6+7-3-2-1)/6 = 16/6 = 2.67

explanations.a: Using only the most likely estimates ignores the probabilistic nature of PERT. PERT's purpose is to weight the most likely estimate 4× and account for the optimistic and pessimistic extremes.
explanations.b: PERT CALCULATIONS: ACTIVITY X: Expected = (O + 4M + P)/6 = (3 + 4×5 + 9)/6 = (3+20+9)/6 = 32/6 = 5.33 days; Standard Deviation σ = (P−O)/6 = (9−3)/6 = 6/6 = 1.00 day; ACTIVITY Y: Expected = (2 + 4×4 + 6)/6 = (2+16+6)/6 = 24/6 = 4.00 days; σ = (6−2)/6 = 4/6 = 0.67 day; ACTIVITY Z: Expected = (1 + 4×3 + 7)/6 = (1+12+7)/6 = 20/6 = 3.33 days; σ = (7−1)/6 = 6/6 = 1.00 day; TOTAL EXPECTED DURATION (sequential activities): E_total = 5.33 + 4.00 + 3.33 = 12.67 days; TOTAL STANDARD DEVIATION (variances add for independent sequential activities): Variance_X = 1.00² = 1.00; Variance_Y = 0.67² = 0.44; Variance_Z = 1.00² = 1.00; Total Variance = 1.00 + 0.44 + 1.00 = 2.44; Total SD = √2.44 = 1.56 days; WHAT THIS TELLS THE PM: EXPECTED COMPLETION: 12.67 days (vs. 12 days using only most likely — PERT adds ~0.67 days for risk); PROBABILITY RANGES (using normal distribution approximation): 68% probability: finish between 12.67 − 1.56 = 11.11 days and 12.67 + 1.56 = 14.23 days; 95% probability: finish between 12.67 − 3.12 = 9.55 days and 12.67 + 3.12 = 15.79 days; RISK ASSESSMENT: Activity X and Z each have σ=1.0 day → they have equal uncertainty; Activity Y has σ=0.67 → less uncertain; the PM should pay closest attention to Activities X and Z for risk monitoring.
explanations.c: PERT standard deviation is a straightforward manual calculation: σ = (P−O)/6 for each activity; total σ = √(sum of individual variances). No computer is required for basic PERT calculations.
explanations.d: The project standard deviation is NOT calculated by applying the SD formula to the project totals — it must be calculated at the activity level and then aggregated using the variance addition rule (square root of sum of squared SDs).

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — all charts compared; selecting the best chart for context
questions.text: A PMO is developing a standard for 'which chart to use when' for all project types. Describe the BEST use case for each of the six chart types: Gantt chart, PERT chart, milestone chart, burndown chart, network diagram, and organizational chart — and identify which chart or combination provides the MOST comprehensive schedule visibility for a complex project.

answers.text: Use only the Gantt chart for everything — it is the most comprehensive tracking tool

Gantt: team-level timeline; PERT: probabilistic duration; Milestone: executive-level; Burndown: Agile sprint/release; Network diagram: dependency/critical path; Org chart: team structure. For MOST comprehensive schedule visibility on a complex project: combine Network diagram (for CPM analysis) + Gantt chart (for timeline communication) + milestone chart (for executive reporting) — the three together cover analytical, operational, and governance needs
Use PERT for everything — it is the most statistically rigorous tool
The burndown chart provides the most comprehensive visibility — it is the most modern tracking method

explanations.a: No single chart provides comprehensive schedule visibility at all levels (analytical, operational, governance). A Gantt chart does not calculate critical path; doesn't show statistical duration probability; isn't appropriate for executive governance reporting.
explanations.b: CHART USE CASE FRAMEWORK: GANTT CHART: BEST FOR: team-level schedule communication; showing all activities with durations, progress, and dependencies in a time-scaled format; AUDIENCE: project team, work-stream leads; WHEN TO USE: throughout execution for operational schedule tracking; PERT CHART/ESTIMATING: BEST FOR: estimating activity durations when uncertainty is HIGH; producing probabilistic completion forecasts; AUDIENCE: PM, planners, sponsors who want probability-based forecasts; WHEN TO USE: during planning for novel activities; when schedule risk quantification is needed. MILESTONE CHART: BEST FOR: executive and steering committee reporting; showing high-level project state without operational detail; AUDIENCE: sponsor, steering committee, board; WHEN TO USE: monthly governance reporting; phase gate preparation. BURNDOWN CHART: BEST FOR: Agile sprint and release progress tracking; showing remaining work vs. ideal; AUDIENCE: Agile development team, product owner; WHEN TO USE: during sprints (sprint burndown) and across releases (release burndown). NETWORK DIAGRAM: BEST FOR: dependency analysis; critical path calculation (CPM); float analysis; schedule compression planning; AUDIENCE: PM, planners, schedule analysts; WHEN TO USE: during planning to identify critical path; when schedule compression options must be evaluated. ORGANIZATIONAL CHART: BEST FOR: showing team structure, reporting relationships, and authority; AUDIENCE: all project participants, new team members, stakeholders; WHEN TO USE: created in initiation; updated when team structure changes. COMPREHENSIVE SCHEDULE VISIBILITY COMBINATION: NETWORK DIAGRAM: tells you WHICH activities have zero float and MUST be protected; calculates the critical path; enables schedule compression analysis; GANTT CHART: shows ALL activities in time sequence; tracks progress; communicates the schedule to the team; MILESTONE CHART: gives executives the governance view (are key events on track?); the three charts work at three different levels of analysis: network = analytical; Gantt = operational; milestone = governance.
explanations.c: PERT provides probabilistic estimates — but it doesn't show the timeline, team, or governance status. It is one tool for one specific need (duration uncertainty).
explanations.d: Burndown charts are excellent for Agile sprint/release tracking — but they don't show dependencies, team structure, or the full project timeline with all activities.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — organizational chart; multi-organization projects; governance clarity in complex team structures
questions.text: A project involves four organizations: the client (who authorized the project), a prime contractor (managing the overall delivery), two subcontractors (providing specialized services). The project org chart must show how these four organizations relate. What design considerations are most important?

answers.text: Only show the prime contractor's team — external organizations create chart complexity
List all organizations in alphabetical order — alphabetical creates fairness

The org chart should: (1) show the CLIENT at the top (they are the authorizing organization — all work is ultimately for them); (2) show the PRIME CONTRACTOR reporting to the client (contractual accountability); (3) show SUBCONTRACTORS reporting to the prime contractor (not directly to the client — the prime is responsible for subcontractor performance); (4) use different visual elements (colors, borders, or labels) to distinguish organizational affiliation; (5) show which prime contractor PM is the single point of contact for the client; this governance structure prevents client organizations from issuing direct instructions to subcontractors (bypassing the prime)
All four organizations should report directly to the project manager — flat hierarchies simplify multi-org projects

explanations.a: An org chart that shows only the prime contractor's team misrepresents the project's governance structure to all parties. The client needs to know who manages the subcontractors; the subcontractors need to know their reporting chain.
explanations.b: Alphabetical listing shows membership but no governance — it doesn't show accountability, reporting relationships, or contractual hierarchy.
explanations.c: MULTI-ORGANIZATION ORG CHART DESIGN: CLIENT POSITION: at the top — the client is the contracting party and ultimate project beneficiary; the client's project sponsor or representative should be clearly identified; PRIME CONTRACTOR POSITION: reporting to the client; the prime contractor has full accountability to the client for all deliverables — including those delivered by subcontractors; the prime contractor's PM is the CLIENT'S single point of contact; SUBCONTRACTORS POSITION: reporting to the prime contractor; NOT reporting directly to the client; this is essential: if the client issues direct instructions to a subcontractor, the prime loses visibility and control; formal instructions must flow through the prime; ORGANIZATIONAL DISTINCTION: use clearly labeled boxes with organizational names; different color coding or border styles to distinguish organizations visually; clear labels: 'CLIENT TEAM', 'PRIME CONTRACTOR TEAM', 'SUBCONTRACTOR A', 'SUBCONTRACTOR B'; GOVERNANCE IMPLICATION: the org chart communicates: client can direct the prime contractor PM; the prime contractor PM directs subcontractors; client should not direct subcontractors without prime awareness; if client wants something from a subcontractor, they request through the prime PM — this protects the prime's coordination and contract management. INTEGRATION TEAM APPROACH: many large multi-org projects have a JOINT PROJECT MANAGEMENT TEAM — representatives from each organization working together, shown as a team reporting to the prime contractor PM.
explanations.d: All four organizations reporting directly to 'the project manager' creates ambiguity about which project manager (the client's or the prime's?) and obscures contractual accountability relationships.

questions.name: Tools and Documentation
questions.keyword: Tracking charts — Gantt chart; maintaining accuracy; forecast vs. baseline; schedule management
questions.text: A project manager updates the Gantt chart weekly. She has been showing only ACTUAL progress (what has been completed) without updating the FORECAST for remaining work. Team leads question why the end date isn't moving when activities are running late. What is wrong with her Gantt maintenance approach?
